content: The pinworm, scientifically classified under the genus Enterobius, is a parasitic roundworm (nematode) that commonly infects the human gastrointestinal tract. It is also referred to as threadworm in the United Kingdom and Australia, or seatworm. The medical condition caused by pinworm infestation is termed enterobiasis, which is a type of helminthiasis. In some cases, it is also referred to as oxyuriasis, named after the family Oxyuridae. It is important to note that in British terminology, the term pinworm may refer to Strongyloides, while Enterobius is called threadworm. Classification The genus Enterobius includes three identified species of pinworms. Humans are exclusively hosts to Enterobius vermicularis (formerly known as Oxyurias vermicularis). Chimpanzees, on the other hand, are hosts to Enterobius anthropopitheci, which is morphologically distinct from the human pinworm. There is some debate regarding the existence of a third species, Enterobius gregorii, which has been proposed as a sister species to E. vermicularis. This species is said to have a slightly smaller spicule (a male reproductive structure). However, its status as a distinct species remains controversial. Some researchers argue that E. gregorii represents a younger developmental stage of E. vermicularis. Clinically, E. gregorii is considered identical to E. vermicularis. Morphology The adult female pinworm is characterized by a sharply pointed posterior end, measuring 8 to 13 mm in length and approximately 0.5 mm in thickness. The adult male is significantly smaller, measuring 2 to 5 mm in length and about 0.2 mm in thickness, with a curved posterior end. Pinworm eggs are translucent, with a sticky surface that allows them to adhere to various objects. These eggs are oval-shaped, measuring 50 to 60 μm in length and 20 to 30 μm in width, with a thick shell that is flattened on one side. Due to their small size and colorless appearance, the eggs are invisible to the naked eye unless present in large clumps. Eggs may contain either a developing embryo or a fully developed pinworm larva. The larvae grow to a size of approximately 140–150 μm. Distribution Pinworms are distributed worldwide and are the most common helminthic infection in the United States, western Europe, and Oceania. In the United States, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reported an overall infection rate of 11.4% across all age groups. Pinworm infections are particularly prevalent among children, with reported rates as high as 61% in India, 50% in England, 39% in Thailand, 37% in Sweden, and 29% in Denmark. Behaviors such as finger-sucking and nail-biting are associated with increased incidence and relapse rates. Pinworm infections are common in households where individuals live in close contact, as the parasite spreads easily through contamination. The prevalence of pinworms is not influenced by gender, social class, race, or culture. Unlike many other intestinal parasites, pinworms are frequently found in affluent communities. Evidence of pinworm infections in humans dates back to ancient times, with pinworm eggs discovered in fossilized human feces from 7837 BC in western Utah. Additionally, parasitic pinworm nematodes were found to have infested pre-mammalian cynodonts approximately 240 million years ago, as evidenced by fossilized eggs in ancient dung. Lifecycle The lifecycle of the pinworm occurs entirely within the gastrointestinal tract of a single human host and spans approximately 2 to 4 weeks, or up to 4 to 8 weeks. The cycle begins when pinworm eggs are ingested. The eggs hatch in the duodenum (the first part of the small intestine), and the emerging larvae grow rapidly to a size of 140 to 150 μm. The larvae migrate through the small intestine toward the colon, undergoing two molts during this migration to reach adulthood. Male and female pinworms mate in the ileum (the last part of the small intestine). After mating, the male pinworms die and are excreted in the stool. Gravid (egg-carrying) female pinworms attach to the mucosa of the ileum, cecum (the beginning of the large intestine), appendix, and ascending colon, where they feed on colonic contents. A gravid female pinworm can carry an estimated 11,000 to 16,000 eggs. Approximately five weeks after the initial ingestion of eggs, the gravid females migrate through the colon toward the rectum at a rate of 12 to 14 cm per hour. They emerge from the anus to deposit their eggs on the perianal skin. This process may occur through contraction and expulsion of eggs, disintegration of the female worm, or rupture of the worm's body due to host scratching. After depositing the eggs, the female pinworm becomes opaque and dies. The emergence of the female from the anus is thought to be necessary for the eggs to mature in the presence of oxygen. Infection The medical condition caused by E. vermicularis is known as enterobiasis. The primary symptom of this condition is intense itching in the anal region. First-line treatments for pinworm infections include albendazole or mebendazole. Pyrantel pamoate is an alternative treatment option. Transmission Pinworms are transmitted through human-to-human contact, primarily via ingestion of infectious eggs or through anal insertion. The eggs are highly resilient and can remain viable in moist environments for up to three weeks. They are sensitive to heat but can survive in cold temperatures, with two-thirds of the eggs remaining viable after 18 hours at −8°C (18°F). Once deposited near the anus, the eggs are easily transferred to other surfaces due to their sticky outer layer. They can contaminate fingernails, hands, clothing, bed linens, food, water, furniture, toys, and bathroom fixtures. Household pets may carry the eggs on their fur, although they are not infected by the parasite. Dust containing eggs can become airborne and inhaled, leading to ingestion. While pinworms do not multiply within the human host, some larvae may hatch on the anal mucosa and migrate back into the gastrointestinal tract in a process known as retroinfection. Retroinfection can result in a heavy parasitic load and prolong the infestation. Autoinfection, where the host reinfects themselves through the anus-to-mouth route or retroinfection, often necessitates repeated treatment at two-week intervals to completely eradicate the infection.
